lesson.title: Conformity, obedience and bystanders

steps.headline: Matching lines in a room of strangers

lead.text: The first set of experiments was run by Solomon Asch in the 1950s. A volunteer joined a small group for what was described as an eyesight test. Everyone looked at one line and at three comparison lines, and said aloud which comparison matched. The right answer was obvious, and people working alone got it wrong on fewer than one judgement in a hundred.

What the volunteer did not know was that everyone else was an actor working for the experimenter, called a confederate. On some rounds the confederates all gave the same wrong answer before the volunteer's turn. Those are the critical trials, and what the volunteer said on one is a critical answer. Giving the group's wrong answer when your own eyes say otherwise is conformity.

afterFigure.text: About 37 critical answers in every 100 followed the wrong majority, and about 75 people in every 100 went along at least once. To get a rate, divide the critical answers that conformed by all the critical answers. Ten people facing 8 critical trials each give 10 × 8 = 80 critical answers, and if 24 followed the majority the rate is 24 ÷ 80 = 30%.

model.setting: Asch's majority condition, about 37 in every 100 critical answers
Asch's majority condition, about 75 in every 100 people

lead.text: A replication of the line task used 18 people. Each gave 12 critical answers, and 72 of all those answers followed the wrong majority.

Asch showed that a group can change what people say. In 1961 Stanley Milgram, a psychologist at Yale, asked what happens when an authority simply tells someone to continue. Volunteers were told they were helping with a study of learning. As the teacher, each had to give a learner an electric shock for every wrong answer, raising the voltage with each mistake, up to a switch marked 450 volts.

The learner was an actor and the shocks were not real, though the volunteers believed they were. As the learner protested and then fell silent, many volunteers hesitated. An experimenter in a grey lab coat answered with calm instructions such as “Please continue.” Obedience is following the instructions of someone you accept as an authority, and Milgram measured it as the share of volunteers who went all the way to the 450-volt switch.
Before the study, people asked to predict the result expected very few to go that far. In the first version, with the learner in another room, most did.
In the first version, with the learner in another room, 26 of the 40 volunteers went on to the final 450-volt switch.

Milgram then moved the learner nearer to see whether distance mattered. At first the learner was in another room and could only be heard. Next he sat in the same room as the volunteer. Closest of all, the volunteer had to press the learner's hand onto a shock plate with their own.

afterFigure.text: Each step closer lowered obedience. In the same room, 16 of 40 went to the end, and with the hand on the plate, 12 of 40 did. To compare two conditions, turn each count into a percentage of its own group and subtract. The difference is in percentage points, so a rate that falls from 50% to 40% has fallen 10 percentage points. Closeness weakened obedience without removing it.

lead.text: The closest version had the volunteer press the learner's hand onto the plate. Compare it with the learner in another room.

steps.headline: How the results have held up

lead.text: Milgram's numbers have been checked, and the checks add detail. Modern ethics rules forbid running his study as it was. In 2009 Jerry Burger ran a version that stopped at 150 volts, the point beyond which most of Milgram's volunteers had gone on to the end. Burger found 70% willing to continue past 150 volts, against 82.5% in Milgram's comparable condition.

A gap that small leaves the main finding standing. Another line of work asks how far the original percentages can be trusted. Gina Perry, an author who went through Milgram's archives, found that experimenters sometimes left the script and pushed volunteers harder than planned, and that many volunteers doubted the shocks were real. A volunteer who suspects the shocks are fake tells you less about obedience.

The careful reading is that obedience to authority is real and weakens with closeness. The exact percentages depend on the setting and on what volunteers believed was happening, so a figure like 65% belongs to one setting and should be quoted with it.

steps.headline: Why a crowd can mean less help

lead.text: Back on the platform, a crowd has two effects that pull in opposite directions. More people means more chances that somebody helps. It can also make each person less likely to help, because everyone can see that others could act and responsibility feels shared out. Psychologists call that diffusion of responsibility.

John Darley and Bibb Latané tested it in 1968. Volunteers joined an intercom discussion, each alone in a separate room. One speaker seemed to have a seizure. Volunteers who believed they were the only listener helped 85% of the time. Volunteers who believed four others were listening helped 31% of the time. Every volunteer was alone in a room, so the difference came from what they believed about the other listeners.
Those percentages are chances for one person. Whether anyone helps depends on how the individual chances add up across the group, and the next screen works that out.

Suppose each person in a crowd decides independently, which means one person's choice does not change another's. The chance that at least one of them acts is easiest to find through the opposite event, that nobody acts. If each of three people acts with probability 0.3, each fails to act with probability 0.7.

Nobody acts only if all three fail, and for independent people you multiply their chances: 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.7 = 0.343. So the chance that at least one acts is 1 − 0.343 = 0.657, or 65.7%. For n people who each act with probability p, the rule is 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ.

afterFigure.text: A lone witness with probability 0.85 beats three witnesses at 0.3 each, whose group chance is 65.7%. A larger crowd gives more chances, but the group does better only if each person's own chance does not fall too far.

lead.text: Two people watch the same emergency. Each decides alone, and each has a one in two chance of acting.

steps.headline: What cameras saw in real streets

lead.text: Laboratory results like these fed a famous story. In 1964 a woman named Kitty Genovese was killed in New York, and a newspaper reported that 38 neighbours watched and did nothing. The story was used for decades to illustrate the bystander effect. The figure of 38 silent witnesses has since been shown to be largely a myth, and some neighbours did call the police.

A better test is to count what happens in real conflicts. Richard Philpot and colleagues studied CCTV recordings of 219 real street conflicts in three cities. In 91% of them at least one bystander stepped in, and the more people were present the more likely it was that someone did.

That fits the arithmetic of the last screen. Even when each person has only a small chance of acting, several people together make it likely that somebody does. What survives from the laboratory is a claim about the individual, who is somewhat less likely to act when others are present. The old story that a crowd means nobody helps does not survive.
Five bystanders watch a street conflict. Each decides independently, and each acts with probability 0.2.

lesson.orientation: Read the classic social-influence studies by their numbers, together with what replications and critics found.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: On an empty station platform, a stranger collapses in front of you. You are the only person who has seen it, so helping is up to you. On a crowded platform the same stranger collapses in front of forty people, and each of them sees exactly what you would have seen.

It seems obvious that more onlookers means more help. The research is less comfortable, and the same is true of much that other people do to us. Their opinions can change what we say we see. An authority's instruction can lead ordinary people to do things they would refuse alone. A crowd can leave each member feeling that helping is somebody else's job.

This lesson goes through three classic sets of experiments on that influence. Each one gives a number you can calculate, either a percentage of people or a probability. All three have since been checked and criticised. You'll learn to read the numbers and the criticism together.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read classic conformity, obedience and bystander results as rates and probabilities, and say what critics later added.

recap.keyIdea: Groups and authority shift behaviour by measurable amounts, and a bystander's chance of acting falls as the crowd grows. The percentages depend on the setting, and replications and archives refine them.

blocks.text: You found that 72 of 216 critical answers conformed, 33.3%, and that 26 of 40 obeyed to 450 volts. Obedience fell by 35 points when the participant had to touch the victim, and five bystanders at 0.2 each give 67.2%.

recap.nextHook: That completes the course. You can now read a study's numbers and ask what else could explain them.

citations.claim: In Asch's line-judgement studies, confederates gave a unanimous wrong answer on critical trials. Alone, people erred on under 1% of judgements. About 37% of critical answers and about 75% of people conformed at least once. Conformity rate is conforming critical answers divided by all critical answers.
In a replication, 18 people gave 12 critical answers each, and 72 of the 216 followed the wrong majority, 33.3%.

In Milgram's 1963 study, volunteers were told to shock a learner for errors up to 450 volts under an experimenter's instruction. The learner was an actor and no shocks were real. Obedience is measured by the share who went to the final switch.
In Milgram's baseline condition 26 of 40 volunteers went to 450 volts, which is 65%.
Obedience fell as the learner came closer: 26 of 40 with the learner in another room, 16 of 40 in the same room and 12 of 40 with the hand on the plate. Rates are compared in percentage points.
Obedience fell from 65% to 30% between the baseline and touch-proximity conditions, 35 percentage points.

Burger's 2009 partial replication stopped at 150 volts and found 70% willing to continue, against 82.5% in Milgram's comparable condition. Perry's archive work found that experimenters sometimes left the script and many participants doubted the shocks.

Darley and Latané's intercom seizure study found 85% helped when they thought they alone heard it and 31% when they thought four others heard. Diffusion of responsibility lowers each person's chance of acting.
If n people act independently with chance p, at least one acts with chance 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ; three people at 0.3 give 65.7%.
Two independent bystanders each acting with probability 0.5 give a 75% chance that at least one acts.
The 38 silent witnesses to the Genovese murder is largely a myth. Philpot and colleagues' CCTV study of 219 real conflicts found someone intervened in 91%, more often with more bystanders.
Five independent bystanders each acting with probability 0.2 give 1 − 0.8⁵ = 67.2% that at least one acts.
Three bystanders each independently help with probability 0.5. What is the probability, as a percentage, that at least one helps? P(nobody) = 0.5³ = 0.125; P(at least one) = 0.875, or 87.5%.
Which statement fits the evidence from CCTV recordings of real public conflicts? Philpot and colleagues (2020) found intervention in 91% of 219 conflicts, rising with the number of bystanders.

Milgram's baseline had 26 of 40 obeying to the end; the same-room condition had 16 of 40. By how many percentage points did obedience fall? 26/40 = 65% and 16/40 = 40%; 65 − 40 = 25 percentage points.
What percentage of critical answers conformed? Give one decimal place. 18 × 12 = 216 critical answers; 72/216 = 0.333, or 33.3%.
What percentage is that? 26/40 = 0.65, or 65%.

In the baseline condition 26 of 40 obeyed to the end, and in the touch-proximity condition 12 of 40 did. By how many percentage points did obedience fall? 26/40 = 65% and 12/40 = 30%; 65 − 30 = 35 percentage points.
Two bystanders each independently act with probability 0.5. What is the probability, as a percentage, that at least one acts? 1 − 0.5² = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75, or 75%.
What is the probability, as a percentage, that at least one acts? Give one decimal place. P(nobody acts) = 0.8⁵ = 0.32768; P(at least one) = 1 − 0.32768 = 0.67232, or 67.2%.
In a conformity study, 21 of 60 critical answers follow the wrong majority. What percentage conformed? 21/60 = 0.35, or 35%.
Two bystanders each independently act with probability 0.4. What is the probability, as a percentage, that at least one acts? 1 − 0.6² = 1 − 0.36 = 0.64, or 64%.
